title: Overview and justification
body:
This course treats reflective practice as exactly that: a professional practice. By now you know what reflection is and you can run a structured reflective cycle. The question this course takes up is how a graduate sustains and owns reflection across a career, using it to critically examine their own practice and to drive their own development.

By the end you will be able to articulate how reflective practice drives self-regulated professional development, use a structured cycle to examine your own experience critically rather than descriptively, and produce critical reflective writing that evaluates your practice and justifies how you will develop it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: articulate how reflective practice drives self-regulated professional and graduate development
use a structured reflective cycle to critically examine your own professional experience
produce critical reflective writing that evaluates your practice and justifies how you will develop it.

title: In real academic practice
body: Reflective practice is not a study exercise you leave behind at graduation; it is the habit professional bodies and employers expect you to carry into practice and sustain for a career. Every appraisal, every supervision conversation, every revalidation or CPD record draws on the same discipline: examining your own practice honestly, weighing it, and acting on what you find. Treat what follows as being about your own emerging professional practice, not about reflection in the abstract.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, reflection as professional practice: why reflection is the engine of self-regulated professional development, and what owning it demands of you. Second, structured critical reflection: using Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle to reflect critically on an experience rather than merely describe it. Third, critical reflective writing: putting that reflection into writing that evaluates your practice and justifies how you will develop. Each lesson builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You already know what reflection is, and you can run a reflective cycle. This lesson steps back to ask a different question: why does any of it matter once you are a practitioner? The answer is that reflection is the mechanism by which professionals keep developing after no one is setting them assignments. This lesson reframes reflection as professional practice, so that it becomes something you own rather than something you are asked to produce.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the aim is not to learn what reflection is but to take ownership of it. You are close to professional practice, where development is self-directed and the standards are set by your field, not a tutor. Expect to appraise reflective practice critically, to judge where it is done well and where it is mere compliance, and to decide what sustaining it will demand of you.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: articulate how reflective practice underpins lifelong, self-regulated professional development
critically appraise a practitioner's reflective approach in a worked example
evaluate what treating reflection as professional practice demands of you in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Self-regulated learning has three phases: setting goals, monitoring your performance against them, and evaluating that performance so you can improve. Reflective practice is the engine of that third phase. To evaluate honestly is to look back critically at your own actions and decisions in order to understand yourself better and act differently next time. Development as a learner, and ultimately into a graduate professional, is driven by this self-reflection.

What makes it professional practice, rather than a study skill, is its scope and its ownership. It does not end at graduation: professional bodies expect you to keep reflecting, recording and developing throughout a career. And no one sets it for you. The self-regulating professional sets their own goals, judges their own performance against them, and decides what to change. Reflection is how that judgement is made.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent time you were responsible for your own performance, in work, placement or study. Did you evaluate it critically afterwards, or move straight on? What would owning reflection as a professional habit change about how you work?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Reflective practice is the engine of self-regulated professional development: the evaluation phase in which you look back critically at your own performance in order to improve, and keep doing so across a career. You can now articulate why it matters, appraise how well a practitioner reflects, and judge what owning it demands of you. The next lesson gives you a structure, Kolb's cycle, for reflecting critically on a single experience.

title: Orientation
body: Reflection only develops you if it is more than a retelling of events. This lesson gives you a structure that forces the step from description to critical reflection: David Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle. The cycle is widely used in professional practice precisely because it does not let you stop at what happened.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have met reflective cycles before. At this level the work is to use one critically: not to march through its stages as a form to fill in, but to let each stage do real analytical work on an experience that matters to you. Expect to integrate theory and concepts into your reflection and to defend the plan you reach.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: apply Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle to structure a critical reflection on an experience
distinguish critical reflection from mere description of what happened
integrate concepts into a reasoned plan for your next cycle of practice in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle treats experience as the currency of learning and gives it four stages. Concrete experience is the thing that happened. Reflective observation is looking back on it: what you noticed, felt and did. Abstract conceptualisation is where the critical work lives, connecting the experience to ideas, theory or professional standards so you understand why it went as it did. Active experimentation is deciding what you will do differently, which becomes the next concrete experience.

The cycle matters because it structures the move from description to critical reflection. A description stops after the first two stages: this happened, and here is how I felt. Critical reflection carries on, drawing on concepts to explain the experience and reaching a reasoned plan for change. The structure is what stops reflection collapsing into storytelling.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Take an experience from your own practice or study that did not go as you expected. Run it quickly through Kolb's four stages in your head. Where did you naturally stop, and what did the later stages make you see that you would otherwise have missed?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Kolb's cycle turns an experience into learning by carrying it through four stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Used critically, it forces the step from describing what happened to explaining it with concepts and planning what to change. You can now structure a reflection with the cycle, tell critical reflection from description, and reach a reasoned plan. The next lesson turns this into writing.

instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 225 to 229 of Chapter 12, 'Learning by Doing: Practice- and Work-Based Learning', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: Professionally, reflection usually has to be written: for a portfolio, a placement log, an appraisal or a revalidation record. This lesson is about what makes reflective writing critical rather than merely descriptive, and how to produce writing that evaluates your own practice and justifies how you will develop.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: Reflective writing is less formal than an essay and is focused almost entirely on your own experience, which can tempt a writer into simple narration. At this level the work is to keep the writing evaluative: to weigh your own actions with evidence and reach justified conclusions, not to tell a story about what happened.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: produce reflective writing that critically evaluates your own actions rather than narrating them
justify developmental conclusions with evidence drawn from your experience
appraise a piece of reflective writing in {{context}} against professional-practice criteria.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Reflective writing stands apart from other academic genres in two ways: it is less formal in style, and it is focused almost exclusively on experience. That focus is the trap. The weakest reflective writing simply describes what happened, faithfully but without judgement. Critical reflective writing does more: it evaluates the writer's own actions, weighs them against evidence and standards, and reaches a justified conclusion about what to develop.

A reliable structure is to move from experience, to reflection, to action: what happened, what you make of it when you weigh it critically, and what you will therefore do differently. Writing that attempts a genuine critical assessment of its own actions, rather than a retelling, is what professional readers are looking for.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Find a short piece of reflective writing you have produced, or imagine one you might write about a recent experience. Does it evaluate your actions, or mostly narrate them? What single change would make it more critical?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Critical reflective writing evaluates your own actions rather than narrating them: it weighs what you did against evidence and standards and justifies a conclusion about how you will develop. You can now write reflection that judges rather than tells, support your conclusions with evidence from your experience, and appraise a piece of reflective writing against professional criteria. You now have the stance, the structure and the writing to sustain reflective practice as a professional.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Reflective practice is no longer something you do for a module; it is a professional discipline you can own. You can articulate why reflection drives self-regulated professional development and what sustaining it asks of you. You can take an experience and run it through Kolb's cycle to reach a reasoned plan, rather than stopping at a description of what happened. And you can put that reflection into writing that evaluates your practice and justifies how you will develop. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, reflective practice belongs to your professional life. Each placement debrief, each appraisal, each supervision conversation and CPD entry is the same discipline at work: examining your practice honestly, weighing it against the standards of your field, and acting on what you find. The graduates who keep developing are the ones who keep reflecting critically, and who can show, in writing, that they do.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two newly qualified practitioners reflecting on the same difficult episode from their first weeks in post.

{{learner-a}} writes up the episode because the portfolio requires it. The account says what happened, in order, and notes that it was stressful and that things turned out acceptably. It is honest and complete, but it treats the reflection as a task to discharge: nothing is weighed, no reason is given for why the episode went as it did, and nothing changes as a result. Reflection here is compliance.

{{learner-b}} writes up the same episode as a professional examining their own practice. They ask why they acted as they did, weigh their decision against what they now know they could have done, and connect it to a standard their field expects. They reach a specific conclusion about what to change and commit to it. The episode becomes development, not a record.

Both practitioners reflected. Only {{learner-b}} treated reflection as professional practice, using it to understand themselves and drive their own improvement.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students reflect on the same group project that went badly when a deadline was missed.

{{learner-a}} stops after the first two stages of the cycle. They describe the experience, the missed deadline and the tension it caused, and observe that they felt frustrated and that communication was poor. The reflection is accurate, but it ends at observation: no concept is brought in to explain it, and no plan follows. It is a description with feelings attached.

{{learner-b}} carries the same experience through all four stages. After describing and observing, they reach abstract conceptualisation: drawing on ideas about group roles and conflict, they recognise that no one had owned coordination and that avoidance let a small slip grow. Then active experimentation: next time they will agree roles and a check-in at the outset. The plan becomes the start of the next cycle.

Both began from the same experience. Only {{learner-b}} used the whole cycle, turning an event into a concept-led plan rather than a retelling.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two placement students write a reflective entry about the same event: a piece of advice they gave that a client did not take.

{{learner-a}} writes: I explained the options clearly and recommended the first one. The client chose differently. I was disappointed, but I respected their decision and moved on. This is faithful narration. It reports the sequence and a feeling, but it never asks whether the advice or the way it was given could have been better, and it reaches no conclusion about the writer's own practice.

{{learner-b}} writes: I recommended the first option, but on reflection I presented it as the obvious choice rather than setting out the trade-offs, which may have made the client feel steered rather than informed. Guidance on shared decision-making suggests the opposite approach. I will next time lay out the options evenly and check the client's priorities before recommending. This evaluates the writer's own actions against a standard and justifies a specific change.

Both described the event. Only {{learner-b}} produced critical reflective writing: evaluative, evidenced, and ending in a justified plan.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What reflective practice asks of a professional
body: Four ideas about reflection as professional practice. Turn each card to see past the common misreading.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: Reflection written only to satisfy a portfolio is compliance. As professional practice, reflection exists to develop you: its test is whether your practice changes, not whether the box is ticked.

No one sets professional reflection for you. The self-regulating professional chooses what to examine, sets the standard, and decides what to change. Ownership is what separates it from a student task.

Self-regulated learning runs on goals, monitoring and evaluation. Reflective practice is that evaluation phase: looking back critically at your performance against the goals you set, so you can improve.
Reflection does not stop at graduation. Appraisal, supervision and revalidation all rest on it. Treating it as professional practice now builds the habit a career will require.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The four stages of Kolb's cycle
body: The four stages of Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, and the work each one does. Open each to see the move.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Concrete experience
_items.body: The thing that happened: a placement episode, a group project, a decision you made. Experience is the currency of this kind of learning, so the cycle starts from something real and specific, not a general topic.

_items.title: Reflective observation
_items.body: Looking back on the experience: what you noticed, what you did, how it felt, what others did. A description stops near here. On its own, observation records the experience but does not yet explain it.

_items.title: Abstract conceptualisation
_items.body: The critical heart of the cycle. You connect the experience to ideas, theory or professional standards to understand why it went as it did. This is where reflection becomes analytical rather than anecdotal.

_items.title: Active experimentation
_items.body: Deciding, with reasons, what you will do differently. The plan is grounded in the concepts from the previous stage, and it becomes the next concrete experience, which is why the cycle keeps turning.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What makes reflective writing critical
body: Four features that separate critical reflective writing from narration. Select each tab to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that feature.

_items.title: Evaluative, not narrative
_items.body: Narration reports what happened. Critical reflective writing judges it: was the action sound, what did it rest on, could it have been better? The difference is between telling a story and weighing it.

_items.title: Evidenced
_items.body: A critical reflection supports its judgements. It points to what in the experience justifies the conclusion, and often to a standard, a concept or guidance from the field, rather than asserting a feeling.

_items.title: Honest about the self
_items.body: Because reflective writing focuses on your own experience, it has to examine your own actions, including what did not go well. A critical assessment of yourself, not a flattering account, is what it asks for.

_items.title: Forward-looking
_items.body: It ends in action. The experience-reflection-action structure closes on a justified plan: what, on this evidence, you will do differently. Writing that stops before the plan has not finished the job.

title: Owning reflective practice
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These habits turn reflection from a task into professional practice. Use them on your next real experience.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I chosen to reflect on this, rather than only because it is required?
Have I set the standard I am judging my performance against?
Have I asked why I acted as I did, not just what I did?
Have I weighed my actions honestly, including what did not go well?
Have I reached a specific decision about what to change?
Will my practice actually be different as a result?

title: Reflecting with Kolb's cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these prompts to carry an experience through all four stages rather than stopping at description.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I fixed on a specific concrete experience to reflect on?
Have I observed what happened and how I and others acted?
Have I brought in a concept, theory or standard to explain why it went as it did?
Have I resisted stopping at how it felt?
Have I reached a concrete plan for what to do differently?
Does my plan set up the next turn of the cycle?

title: Writing critical reflection
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these checks to keep reflective writing evaluative rather than narrative.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I evaluated my own actions, not just reported them?
Have I supported each judgement with evidence from the experience?
Have I referred to a standard, concept or guidance from my field?
Have I been honest about what did not go well?
Have I followed the experience-reflection-action structure?
Does the writing end in a justified plan for development?

title: Formative check: why reflective practice matters
displayTitle: Why is reflective practice treated as more than something you do for a single assignment?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is reflective practice more than a one-off assignment task?

_items.text: Because it is the evaluation phase of self-regulated development that professionals sustain across a career.
_items.feedback: Yes. It is how a self-regulating professional keeps evaluating and improving, long after graduation.

_items.text: Because tutors require a reflection to be submitted with most assignments.
_items.feedback: A submission requirement is not what gives reflection its value; its purpose is development.

_items.text: Because it is a quick way to add length to a portfolio.
_items.feedback: Reflection is not padding; it is the mechanism of self-directed improvement.

_items.text: Because it replaces the need to set goals or monitor your work.
_items.feedback: Reflection is the evaluation phase; it works alongside goal-setting and monitoring, not instead of them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflective practice is the evaluation phase of self-regulated development, sustained across a professional career.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what reflection does in the cycle of self-regulated development.
_incorrect.final: Reflective practice matters because it is the evaluation phase of self-regulated development that professionals sustain across a career, not because it is required or adds length.

title: Formative check: appraising a reflection
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second practitioner's reflection professional practice rather than compliance?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second practitioner's reflection professional practice rather than compliance?

_items.text: They weighed their actions against a standard and reached a specific change.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing against a standard and committing to a change is reflection as development.

_items.text: They produced a longer and more detailed account of the episode.
_items.feedback: Length and detail do not make a reflection critical; weighing and change do.

_items.text: They completed the portfolio entry on time.
_items.feedback: Completing the entry is compliance; it is not what made the reflection developmental.

_items.text: They described exactly what happened, in order.
_items.feedback: An ordered description is the compliance approach the first practitioner took.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second practitioner weighed their actions against a standard and reached a specific change.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second practitioner DID beyond recording the episode.
_incorrect.final: It was professional practice because they weighed their actions against a standard and reached a change, not because it was longer, on time, or well ordered.

title: Formative check: owning reflection
displayTitle: You are developing your practice in {{context}}. Which approach treats reflection as professional practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach treats reflection as professional practice?

_items.text: Choosing an episode to examine, judging it against the standards of {{context}}, and deciding what to change.
_items.feedback: Yes. Self-directed, standard-referenced and change-oriented reflection is professional practice in {{context}}.

_items.text: Writing a reflection only when a tutor or supervisor asks for one.
_items.feedback: Reflecting only on request is compliance, not owned professional practice.

_items.text: Recording what happened so there is a complete file.
_items.feedback: A complete record is not the same as a critical reflection that changes your practice.

_items.text: Waiting until you are qualified before reflecting on your work.
_items.feedback: Reflective practice is built now; it is the habit a career in {{context}} will require.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, owned reflection means choosing what to examine, judging it against your field's standards, and acting on it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the self-directed option that judges against a standard and leads to change.
_incorrect.final: Treating reflection as professional practice in {{context}} means self-directed, standard-referenced reflection that changes your practice, not reflecting only on request or merely recording events.

title: Formative check: what the cycle adds
displayTitle: What does Kolb's cycle add to simply thinking back over an experience?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does Kolb's cycle add to thinking back over an experience?

_items.text: It carries the experience through to explaining it with concepts and planning a change.
_items.feedback: Yes. The later stages force conceptualisation and a plan, which thinking back alone often skips.

_items.text: It makes the reflection longer so it looks more thorough.
_items.feedback: The cycle is about structure and depth, not length.

_items.text: It removes the need to describe what happened.
_items.feedback: Description is the first stage; the cycle adds to it rather than removing it.

_items.text: It guarantees the experience will not happen again.
_items.feedback: No cycle guarantees outcomes; it structures how you learn from them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The cycle carries an experience through to concepts and a reasoned plan.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the stages a quick think-back usually leaves out.
_incorrect.final: Kolb's cycle adds abstract conceptualisation and a plan: the stages a quick think-back usually skips. It does not add mere length or remove description.

title: Formative check: critical versus descriptive
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reflection critical rather than descriptive?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's reflection critical rather than descriptive?

_items.text: They explained the episode with concepts and reached a concrete plan for next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Conceptualising the experience and planning a change is what makes it critical.

_items.text: They described the missed deadline and the tension more vividly.
_items.feedback: Vivid description is still description; the first student stopped there.

_items.text: They spent longer feeling frustrated about the outcome.
_items.feedback: Dwelling on a feeling is not critical reflection.

_items.text: They blamed the other group members clearly.
_items.feedback: Assigning blame is not conceptualisation or planning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student used concepts to explain the episode and reached a plan.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the stages the first student left out.
_incorrect.final: It was critical because the second student conceptualised the episode and reached a plan, not because the description was more vivid or the feeling stronger.

title: Formative check: completing the cycle
displayTitle: Reflecting on an experience in {{context}}, you have described it and observed how it went. What does the cycle require next to keep the reflection critical?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does the cycle require next, after describing and observing?

_items.text: Connect it to concepts or standards to explain why it happened, then plan a change.
_items.feedback: Yes. Abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation are what make the reflection critical in {{context}}.

_items.text: Write up the description more fully before moving on.
_items.feedback: Expanding the description keeps you at the observation stage.

_items.text: Record how you felt in more detail.
_items.feedback: More feeling is not the critical move; explanation and planning are.

_items.text: Decide the experience was simply bad luck.
_items.feedback: Attributing it to luck avoids the conceptualisation the cycle asks for.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the critical move is to conceptualise why it happened and plan a change.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which two stages of the cycle come after reflective observation?
_incorrect.final: After describing and observing, the cycle requires abstract conceptualisation and a plan for change. Expanding the description or the feeling keeps the reflection at the observation stage.

title: Formative check: critical versus narrative writing
displayTitle: What distinguishes critical reflective writing from narrative reflective writing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What distinguishes critical from narrative reflective writing?

_items.text: It evaluates the writer's own actions and reaches a justified conclusion, rather than only reporting events.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evaluation and a justified conclusion are what make the writing critical.

_items.text: It uses a more formal academic style throughout.
_items.feedback: Reflective writing is less formal; style is not what makes it critical.

_items.text: It tells the story of the experience in more vivid detail.
_items.feedback: Vivid storytelling is still narration, not critical reflection.

_items.text: It avoids mentioning the writer's own feelings.
_items.feedback: Feelings can appear; the point is to evaluate actions, not to omit feeling.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Critical reflective writing evaluates the writer's own actions and justifies a conclusion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the writing DOES beyond reporting the experience.
_incorrect.final: Critical reflective writing evaluates the writer's own actions and justifies a conclusion. A more formal style, vivid detail or omitted feelings do not make writing critical.

title: Formative check: justified conclusions
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second entry's conclusion justified rather than merely asserted?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second entry's conclusion justified?

_items.text: It weighed the writer's own action against a standard and pointed to evidence from the experience.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evidence from the experience and a standard justify the conclusion.

_items.text: It stated the plan more confidently.
_items.feedback: Confidence is not justification; evidence and a standard are.

_items.text: It described the client's reaction in more detail.
_items.feedback: More description of the client is not what justifies the writer's conclusion.

_items.text: It was written in the first person.
_items.feedback: First person is normal in reflection; it does not justify a conclusion.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The conclusion was justified by evidence from the experience and a professional standard.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second entry offered in support of its conclusion.
_incorrect.final: The conclusion was justified because it weighed the action against a standard and pointed to evidence, not because it was confident, detailed or first-person.

title: Formative check: appraising reflective writing
displayTitle: Appraising a reflective entry about {{context}} against professional-practice criteria, which feature shows it is genuinely critical?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which feature shows a reflective entry is genuinely critical?

_items.text: It evaluates the writer's actions with evidence and ends in a justified plan to develop.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evaluation, evidence and a justified plan are the marks of critical reflective writing in {{context}}.

_items.text: It gives a complete, orderly account of what happened in {{context}}.
_items.feedback: A complete account is narration; on its own it is not critical.

_items.text: It is written in a polished, formal style.
_items.feedback: Polish is not the criterion; evaluation and a justified plan are.

_items.text: It stays positive about the writer's own performance.
_items.feedback: An honest appraisal weighs what did not go well, not only the positives.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Evaluation with evidence, ending in a justified plan, is what makes it critical in {{context}}.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which feature shows weighing and a justified plan, rather than a tidy account?
_incorrect.final: A genuinely critical entry about {{context}} evaluates the writer's actions with evidence and ends in a justified plan. A complete account, a polished style or unbroken positivity do not make it critical.

body: What best explains why reflective practice is treated as a professional practice rather than a study task?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is reflective practice treated as a professional practice?

_items.text: It is self-directed and sustained across a career to drive your own development.
_items.feedback: Yes. Ownership and lifelong development make it professional practice.

_items.text: It is required on most university assignments.
_items.feedback: A requirement does not make it professional practice.

_items.text: It is a quick way to lengthen a portfolio.
_items.feedback: Reflection is not padding.

_items.text: It replaces goal-setting and monitoring.
_items.feedback: It is the evaluation phase, working with goals and monitoring.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflective practice is self-directed and sustained across a career.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about ownership and the span of a career.

body: Reflective practice is the engine of which phase of self-regulated learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Reflective practice is the engine of which phase of self-regulated learning?

_items.text: Evaluation of performance against the goals you set.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflection drives the evaluation phase.

_items.text: Setting the initial goals.
_items.feedback: Goal-setting is a separate phase; reflection evaluates against it.

_items.text: Monitoring behaviour while you work.
_items.feedback: Monitoring is the phase before evaluation.

_items.text: Choosing which module to study.
_items.feedback: That is not a phase of self-regulated learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflective practice drives the evaluation phase.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which phase looks back and judges performance against goals?

body: Which stage does critical reflection add that a plain description of an experience usually omits?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which stage does critical reflection add that description omits?

_items.text: Abstract conceptualisation, explaining the experience with concepts, leading to a plan.
_items.feedback: Yes. Conceptualisation and the plan are what description leaves out.

_items.text: A fuller account of what happened.
_items.feedback: That is still description.

_items.text: A more detailed record of how it felt.
_items.feedback: Feeling sits in observation, not conceptualisation.

_items.text: A note of when and where it happened.
_items.feedback: Context details are still part of description.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Critical reflection adds abstract conceptualisation and a plan.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which Kolb stage explains WHY the experience went as it did?

body: A reflection that stops after describing an event and saying how it felt is missing what?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is a description-and-feeling reflection missing?

_items.text: Conceptualising why it happened and planning what to change.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those later stages are what make reflection critical.

_items.text: A longer description of the event.
_items.feedback: Length is not the missing element.

_items.text: A stronger statement of the feeling.
_items.feedback: More feeling is not what is missing.

_items.text: An apology for the outcome.
_items.feedback: An apology is not a stage of critical reflection.

_feedback.correct: That's right. It is missing conceptualisation and a plan.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the two stages that come after observation.

body: What makes a piece of reflective writing critical rather than narrative?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What makes reflective writing critical rather than narrative?

_items.text: It evaluates the writer's own actions and justifies a conclusion with evidence.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evaluation and a justified conclusion make it critical.

_items.text: It tells the story in vivid, ordered detail.
_items.feedback: Ordered detail is narration.

_items.text: It uses a formal academic register.
_items.feedback: Reflective writing is less formal; register is not the point.

_items.text: It keeps a positive tone about the writer.
_items.feedback: Honest appraisal weighs what did not go well.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Critical reflective writing evaluates actions and justifies a conclusion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the writing does beyond reporting.

body: A critical reflective entry should end with which of these?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How should a critical reflective entry end?

_items.text: A justified plan for development, supported by evidence from the experience.
_items.feedback: Yes. The experience-reflection-action structure closes on a justified plan.

_items.text: A summary of what happened, in order.
_items.feedback: A summary is narration, not a plan.

_items.text: A statement that the experience went well overall.
_items.feedback: A verdict without a plan does not close the reflection critically.

_items.text: A list of everyone else involved.
_items.feedback: Listing others is not a developmental plan.

_feedback.correct: That's right. It ends with a justified, evidenced plan for development.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What does the experience-reflection-action structure close on?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: reflection as professional practice, a structured cycle for reflecting critically, and critical reflective writing. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you own and sustain.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage the aim is not to add a new technique. It is to see the stance, the cycle and the writing as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas, so that reflection carries on into your professional life.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together the professional stance, the structured critical cycle and critical reflective writing as one continuing practice
recognise reflective practice sustained as continuing professional development in a worked example
plan how you will keep reflecting critically on your own practice in {{context}} beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Reflective practice, owned as a professional, is these three strands working as one. The stance is why you do it: reflection drives your own development once no one sets you assignments. The cycle is how you do it critically, carrying an experience through to a reasoned change. The writing is how you evaluate and justify that development on the record. Run together, again and again, they are a single continuing discipline, not three separate tasks.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the three strands run together across your work, not once at the end. You take an experience you own, carry it through the cycle so the reflection is critical, and write it up so it evaluates and justifies a change. Done after each significant experience, with one change carried forward, those rounds compound over a career.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one part of your own practice you could keep reflecting on this year, such as how you handle feedback, group work or a recurring task. What would you look back on, and when would you run the cycle and write it up?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Reflective practice matters most when the three strands run as one continuing discipline. You own the experience, work it through the cycle, and write an evaluation that justifies a change, again and again across your career. It is the repeated practice, not any single reflection, that develops you as a professional.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: The stance, the cycle and the writing run together as one continuing discipline, not three separate tasks. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Take ownership
_items.body: Take ownership of an experience from your own practice as something worth developing from.

_items.title: Reflect critically
_items.body: Run it through the reflective cycle, reflecting critically rather than describing what happened.

_items.title: Write it up
_items.body: Write it up as an evaluation that weighs your actions and justifies one change.

_items.title: Carry forward
_items.body: Carry that change into your next piece of practice, then reflect on it again. The cycle keeps turning.

_diagram.title: Reflective practice as a continuing discipline

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two practitioners get the same hard feedback early in their first post. One treats each new task as a fresh start and keeps meeting the same problem. The other owns it, runs it through the cycle, writes an honest evaluation, and carries one change into the next task. Over the year the second practitioner's work improves, because the three strands ran as one practice.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep reflecting as a professional
body: Use these to keep the three strands running as one continuing practice, not as separate tasks.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I treated this reflection as my own development, not a task set for me?
Have I carried the experience through the whole cycle, not stopped at describing it?
Have I weighed my own actions against the standards of my field?
Have I written it up so it evaluates and justifies, rather than narrates?
Have I carried one change forward into my next piece of practice?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat the stance, the cycle and the writing as one continuing practice rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it better to treat the stance, the cycle and the writing as one continuing practice rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat the stance, the cycle and the writing as one continuing practice rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because each strand feeds the next: the stance makes you reflect, the cycle makes the reflection critical, and the writing records a change you then carry back into practice.
_items.feedback: Yes. Run together, each strand feeds the next, so the practice develops you over a career.

_items.text: Because doing all three once, in detail, settles your development for good.
_items.feedback: A single round rarely develops practice. Reflection works when the whole loop repeats.

_items.text: Because keeping them separate means you never have to judge your own actions.
_items.feedback: Owning reflection means judging your own actions. That is the point of the stance.

_items.text: Because one continuing practice takes less thought than running the three strands.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. A habit spreads the work so it stays sustainable.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Run together, each strand feeds the next, so reflection keeps developing your practice across a career.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by running the stance, the cycle and the writing as one repeating loop.

displayTitle: A newly qualified practitioner owns a difficult episode, runs it through the cycle to reach a change, writes it up as an evaluation, and applies the change next time. What does this show?
body: A newly qualified practitioner owns a difficult episode, runs it through the cycle to reach a change, writes it up as an evaluation, and applies the change next time. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A newly qualified practitioner owns a difficult episode, runs it through the cycle to reach a change, writes it up as an evaluation, and applies the change next time. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three strands work as one practice: the stance, the cycle and the writing together produced a change that improved the next experience.
_items.feedback: Yes. The whole loop ran: own it, reflect critically, write the evaluation, carry the change forward.

_items.text: That the practitioner simply described the episode in more detail than before.
_items.feedback: Describing is only the start. Here the practitioner evaluated and changed, which is the practice.

_items.text: That writing the reflection down was the only part that mattered.
_items.feedback: The writing records the work, but the stance and the cycle did the reflecting first.

_items.text: That the episode would now never happen again.
_items.feedback: Reflection does not guarantee that. It changes how you act and keep developing.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Owning it, reflecting through the cycle, writing the evaluation and applying the change is the whole practice at work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what the practitioner did across the whole loop, not any single step.

displayTitle: You want to use this continuing practice to keep developing in {{context}} this year. Which plan best keeps all three strands running as one?
body: You want to use this continuing practice to keep developing in {{context}} this year. Which plan best keeps all three strands running as one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this continuing practice to keep developing in your subject this year. Which plan best keeps all three strands running as one?

_items.text: After each significant experience in {{context}}, own it, run it through the cycle, write an evaluation that justifies one change, and apply that change next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the stance, the cycle and the writing together, again and again.

_items.text: Write one long reflection on {{context}} at the end of the year, covering everything at once.
_items.feedback: One reflection at the end cannot change practice you have already finished.

_items.text: Reflect only on the parts of {{context}} that went badly, to avoid dwelling on them.
_items.feedback: Critical reflection weighs what went well too, not only what went wrong.

_items.text: Note how each experience in {{context}} felt, without deciding on any change.
_items.feedback: Noticing how it felt is a start, but the practice needs an evaluated change.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Owning each experience, reflecting through the cycle and writing an evaluated change keeps all three strands running as one.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps the stance, the cycle and the writing going together over time.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What best explains why reflective practice is treated as one continuing discipline rather than three separate tasks?
body: What best explains why reflective practice is treated as one continuing discipline rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best explains why reflective practice is treated as one continuing discipline rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because the stance, the cycle and the writing feed one another and are repeated across a career.
Because each of the three is assessed separately by a tutor.
Because writing is the only part that counts professionally.
Because reflecting once in depth settles your development for good.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A practitioner owns a setback, runs it through the cycle to a reasoned change, and records an evaluation that justifies it. What does this best show?
body: A practitioner owns a setback, runs it through the cycle to a reasoned change, and records an evaluation that justifies it. What does this best show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A practitioner owns a setback, runs it through the cycle to a reasoned change, and records an evaluation that justifies it. What does this best show?

_items.text: Reflective practice working as one continuing discipline, from the professional stance through to justified, written development.
That the practitioner prefers writing to reflecting.
That the setback was not really the practitioner's responsibility.
That a single reflection has now completed their development.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
